Selig’s death was as slow as a funeral procession. The whole week after his wounding, his condition worsened.

The whole time, he heard himself called by a name he did not like; the name of his enemy.

Late in the evening of the seventh day, he heard a new voice, one that had not called him by that name.

He saw the doctor.

He was a bit taller than himself. He was dressed in a long, dark cloak and carried a heavy wooden stick, which looked more like a walking stick than a cane.

He was an old man.

Selig was sure of it. The light from the lamp cast a shadow across his face. Selig could not see that face; and yet he knew that it was old, very old.

“The old man!” Selig whispered, not realizing he had uttered the words aloud.

“Hmm?” The old man turned toward the voice.

He did not look around. His head swiveled. A few of his white hairs fell down into his dark eyes.

He moved his stick aside. “What did you say?”

“The Old Man,” Selig said. “I thought you were the old man.”

The old man raised an eyebrow. His eyes were kind, but they were dark, like his cloak. “You are very confused. You do not remember me.”

“No.” Selig felt tears starting in his eyes, and was afraid to look away from the old man.

The old man smiled. It was a kindly smile; not a mocking one.

“It’s all right,” the old man said. “It will come back to you.”

“I need to know.” Selig gripped the blanket around him, as if that would warm him. “I have to know what I am. What I was, before. What I will be, when I die.”

The old man nodded. “You do indeed. But it is not that you will be. You already are.”

“I am?” Selig felt his heart beating in his chest. “What am I?”

The old man sighed. “What do you wish to be?”

Selig had a sudden vision: he was a dog, a dog in the snow. He was alone, and there was no one to care for him.

He did not like that idea.

He shook the image from his mind. He sat up in bed. “I want to be… I want to be…”

“You can’t be anything.” The old man looked at him sadly. “You are already what you are.”

“Then what am I?”

The old man raised his stick and pointed it toward Selig. “You are the golem.”

“The golem?” Selig knew what a golem was. He was supposed to be one. “But I’m not.”

“You are a golem,” the old man insisted. “There is no doubt about it.”

“But I’m not. I’m a man. A man who was supposed to be a golem. I’m just a failure. I failed. That’s all.”

The old man shook his head. “Not a failure. You were made to be a golem.”

“I am not a golem.” Selig looked around for something to help him stand up. He fell back in the bed, and the blanket moved down. He was naked beneath it, and his chest was scarred. He could not tell if there was a bullet there or not.

The old man sighed again. “We can’t talk if you are in bed.”

Selig was ashamed. He sat up, and the old man turned away. Selig dressed himself in the tattered remnants of his uniform. He was a failure. He was a dog in the snow. He was nothing.

He took the old man by the hand, and he led the old man toward the door.

The old man shook his head. “This way.”

The old man led Selig into a dark hallway. It was an ancient hallway, with old stone walls and wooden rails. It was a passageway between two buildings, and on the other side of it was a garden.

The old man led Selig to the middle of the garden, then sat down on the grass. The grass was short, and cool to the touch. It was as bright as the stars.

Selig stood in the middle of the garden, looking out over the land around it. He had never seen anything like it before.

“Where are we?” Selig asked.

The old man looked at him, and smiled. “Where are we?”

“Yes. Where are we?”

The old man stood up, and came to Selig. He took his hand again. He felt as if it were a human hand, but larger, more powerful, and yet more gentle. He looked at the old man’s face, and he saw that he was kind, and wise.

Selig smiled back at the old man. “I… I don’t know.”

The old man nodded. “It is not your home. But it is a very good place to be. You are very welcome.”

The old man turned and walked away. Selig was alone in the garden. He turned around and went back to the house.

He was still thinking about the garden as he went through the front door.

The old man was not there.

The doctor was, however, there. He was waiting for Selig, and he was wearing the same clothes he had worn when he had last seen him.

He smiled at Selig. “Hello, Selig.”

Selig looked at him. He was an older version of himself. “What did you say?”

The doctor smiled. “I said hello, Selig. How are you feeling?”

Selig looked at him. “I’m feeling… I’m feeling good. I’m feeling very well.”

The doctor smiled. “Good. You’ve had a very hard week.”

Selig nodded. “Yes. Yes, I have.”

The doctor nodded. “And it’s only Tuesday.”

Selig frowned. “What do you mean?”

The doctor smiled. “I mean that you have another hard week to look forward to. I mean you have another six days to go.”

Selig nodded. “I guess I do. I guess I do.”

“You’re going to feel better.” The doctor shook his head. “You are going to get better. I promise you that.”

Selig nodded. “I… I hope so.”

“Selig.” The doctor looked at him. “I have a favor to ask.”

“Yes?” Selig looked at him.

“I know you don’t want to do it.” The doctor looked at him. “But I need to know if you are still alive.”

Selig nodded. “I am. I’m alive.”

“Good.” The doctor nodded. “I’m glad to hear it.”

Selig looked at him. “Do you need to know if I’m going to die?”

The doctor shook his head. “No. No, I don’t.”

“Then why?” Selig asked. “Why do you need to know?”

The doctor smiled. “Because I’m trying to find out what you are.”

Selig nodded. “I’m a golem.”

The doctor nodded. “Yes. You are.”

Selig looked at him. “And?”

The doctor smiled. “And what?”

Selig shook his head. “I don’t know.”

The doctor nodded. “Good. Good. Let’s talk about that.”

Selig nodded. “All right.”

The doctor sat down on the bed next to Selig. “Selig, I want to talk to you about your condition.”

Selig nodded. “Yes?”

The doctor smiled. “You’re in a lot of pain. You’re in a lot of pain because of what happened to you.”

Selig looked at him. “What happened to me?”

The doctor shook his head. “I’m not sure.”

“What happened to me?”

Selig nodded. “A miracle.”
